title: DFS on LA Streets: Real Intersections Explored ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “dive” through real street intersections like a stack-powered explorer, going deep before it backtracks. This DFS traversal visualization shows exactly how recursion/stack order changes the path and visit order.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps — what happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡

On a real-street grid, we convert roads to a graph: intersections = nodes, streets = edges. Then DFS uses a stack (or recursion) to go as deep as possible first—so the *neighbor ordering* you choose can completely change the traversal sequence.

In this visualization, notice:
• The “current path” grows downward until it hits a dead end
• Then DFS backtracks and continues from the last branching node
• The visited set prevents infinite loops on cyclic street layouts

✅ Takeaway: DFS is great for exhaustive exploration, but traversal order (and resulting route) depends on your graph representation + neighbor ordering.

Debate question: In a city map, should a traversal prioritize “deep exploration” (DFS) or “shortest expansion” (BFS)?
